technologies.summary: Chemical absorption removes CO₂ from flue or process gas, then heat regenerates the solvent and releases a concentrated CO₂ stream.
technologies.carbon_fate: Capture alone stores nothing. The fate of the carbon is set by the downstream use or storage route.
chemical_reactions: CO₂ + 2 RNH₂ ⇌ RNHCOO⁻ + RNH₃⁺ (carbamate formation, primary amine)
catalysts: No catalyst; amine solvent formulation sets absorption rate, cyclic capacity and degradation
technologies.process_conditions: Absorber near ambient temperature; stripper at elevated temperature with steam. Report solvent, capture rate, CO₂ purity and specific heat duty on one stated boundary.

technical_performance.assumptions: Upper bound for carbamate formation only; operating cyclic loading is lower and solvent-specific

technical_performance.basis: Minimum separation work from 12 mol% CO₂
technical_performance.assumptions: Ideal gas at 298 K and 1 atm, pure CO₂ product, vanishing capture fraction; excludes compression and all real losses

technologies.demonstrated_scale: Amine absorption is established in gas processing; readiness for a specific flue gas, capture rate and site must be shown by that installation.
known_limitations: Regeneration heat demand and its source
Capture rate versus marginal energy penalty
technologies.economics: Cost depends strongly on CO₂ concentration, plant size, heat availability and operating hours. A capture cost excludes conditioning, transport and the downstream use or storage.
technologies.lifecycle_evidence: Count emissions from regeneration heat, electricity and solvent supply. Fossil or biogenic origin of the captured carbon decides what downstream claims are possible.

technologies.summary: Liquid or solid sorbents take CO₂ directly from ambient air; regeneration then delivers concentrated CO₂ for storage or use.
technologies.carbon_fate: Atmospheric origin is necessary but not sufficient for removal: the CO₂ must then be stored durably. Used in fuels, it is re-released.
chemical_reactions: 2 KOH + CO₂ → K₂CO₃ + H₂O (liquid-solvent route, simplified)
catalysts: No catalyst; sorbent chemistry (hydroxide solutions or amine-functionalised solids) controls uptake and regeneration
technologies.process_conditions: Very large air-contacting area. Regeneration ranges from moderate-temperature vacuum/steam swing for solid sorbents to high-temperature calcination for liquid-solvent loops.

technical_performance.assumptions: Ideal gas at 298 K and 1 atm, pure CO₂ product, vanishing capture fraction; real systems need several times more energy

technologies.demonstrated_scale: Pilot and early commercial plants exist; each must be judged on measured net capture over sustained operation.
known_limitations: Energy demand from a very dilute source
Air-contactor capital cost and land use
technologies.economics: Capital-intensive and energy-intensive per tonne. Published cost figures differ in boundary, scale and year; compare only like-for-like delivered-CO₂ costs.
technologies.lifecycle_evidence: Net removal requires subtracting emissions from energy, materials and construction, and durable storage of the delivered CO₂.

technologies.summary: CO₂ and hydrogen react over a copper/zinc-oxide catalyst to make methanol, a fuel and chemical building block.
technologies.carbon_fate: Methanol used as fuel releases its carbon at combustion; methanol converted into durable chemicals or materials holds it longer.
catalysts: Cu/ZnO-based catalyst systems; formulation is process-specific
technologies.process_conditions: Elevated pressure and temperature; report the specific reactor conditions rather than a universal optimum.

technical_performance.assumptions: Complete atom balance; excludes losses and purge

technologies.demonstrated_scale: Project-dependent. No plant-level scale or operational status has been verified in this initial atlas.
known_limitations: Water separation, purge losses and heat integration
technologies.economics: Purchased hydrogen can dominate feedstock cost. Use the transparent scenario model; its partial cost excludes capital recovery and fixed operating expenses.
technologies.lifecycle_evidence: Carbon in fuel is released at use. Climate benefit depends on feedstock origin, displaced production and energy supply; utilization does not establish removal.

technologies.summary: The Sabatier reaction combines CO₂ with hydrogen over a nickel or ruthenium catalyst to make synthetic methane.
technologies.carbon_fate: Carbon returns to the atmosphere when the fuel is combusted, typically within months to a few years of production.
chemical_reactions: CO₂ + 4 H₂ → CH₄ + 2 H₂O (Sabatier, strongly exothermic)
catalysts: Nickel-based catalysts; ruthenium for some applications
technologies.process_conditions: Catalytic route typically operates at a few hundred °C with active heat removal; biological methanation operates near ambient temperature with methanogenic archaea.

technical_performance.assumptions: Complete conversion; excludes slip, purge and losses

technologies.demonstrated_scale: Power-to-gas plants have been built at various scales; operating hours and measured output must be verified per site.
known_limitations: Heat management of the exothermic reaction
Catalyst sensitivity to sulphur and other impurities
technologies.economics: Hydrogen supply dominates. Roughly half the hydrogen ends up as water, so energy efficiency from electricity to methane is lower than for some other e-fuels.
technologies.lifecycle_evidence: Methane slip along the chain can erode benefits; electricity carbon intensity and CO₂ origin determine the result.

technologies.summary: CO₂ is first converted to CO-rich syngas—by reverse water–gas shift or co-electrolysis—then Fischer–Tropsch synthesis builds liquid hydrocarbons such as e-kerosene.
technologies.carbon_fate: Carbon returns to the atmosphere when the fuel is combusted, typically within months to a few years of production.
chemical_reactions: CO₂ + H₂ ⇌ CO + H₂O (reverse water–gas shift)
technologies.process_conditions: RWGS is endothermic and favoured at high temperature; Fischer–Tropsch is exothermic at lower temperature. Product distribution needs hydrocracking and refining.

technical_performance.basis: Ideal net reaction CO₂ + 3 H₂ → –CH₂– + 2 H₂O
technical_performance.assumptions: Complete conversion to a long-chain paraffin unit; excludes light-gas by-products and losses

technologies.demonstrated_scale: Fischer–Tropsch is industrial for fossil syngas; integration with CO₂ and electrolytic hydrogen is at demonstration and first-of-a-kind scale.
technologies.economics: Hydrogen and capital dominate. Compare with fossil jet fuel only on a stated, complete boundary and separate any policy support from production cost.
technologies.lifecycle_evidence: Low-carbon electricity is essential. Fuel-use emissions return the carbon; claims depend on CO₂ origin and the accounting rules applied.

technologies.summary: An electrolyser uses electricity to reduce CO₂ at a cathode to CO, formate, ethylene or other products.
technologies.carbon_fate: Depends on the product: CO or formate for fuels re-release carbon; multicarbon products used in materials hold it longer.
chemical_reactions: CO₂ + 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻ → CO + H₂O (cathode half-reaction)
products: CO or other products, depending on catalyst and reactor
catalysts: Silver-based systems for CO; copper-based systems for multicarbon products
technologies.process_conditions: Specify electrolyte, full-cell voltage, current density, electrode area and operating duration together.

technical_performance.assumptions: Complete conversion; excludes carbonate crossover and other carbon losses
Minimum charge at 100% Faradaic efficiency; energy also requires the full-cell voltage

technologies.demonstrated_scale: Laboratory and larger systems must be assessed individually; no universal pathway TRL is assigned.
technologies.economics: Faradaic efficiency alone does not specify electricity consumption: full-cell voltage, current and production rate are needed.
technologies.lifecycle_evidence: Include electricity and replacement materials; track carbon leaving every outlet, not only the desired product.

technologies.summary: Acetogenic bacteria convert CO, CO₂ and H₂ from industrial off-gas or electrolysis into ethanol and other chemicals.
technologies.carbon_fate: Depends on the product: ethanol used as fuel re-releases carbon quickly; chemicals and polymers made from it hold carbon for their service life.
technologies.process_conditions: Near-ambient temperature in aqueous broth; performance depends on gas–liquid mass transfer, strain and gas impurities.

technical_performance.basis: Ideal net reaction from CO₂ + H₂
technical_performance.assumptions: No biomass growth, by-products or losses

technical_performance.basis: Ideal net reaction from CO₂ + H₂
technical_performance.assumptions: Not actual plant consumption; CO-rich gas routes need less or no added hydrogen

technologies.demonstrated_scale: Commercial plants operate on CO-rich industrial off-gas; CO₂ + H₂ operation must be assessed separately.
known_limitations: Low gas solubility and mass transfer
technologies.economics: Off-gas availability, ethanol prices and separation energy drive the result; CO₂-only routes add hydrogen cost.
technologies.lifecycle_evidence: When using fossil-derived off-gas, the climate benefit is avoided production, not removal. Allocation with the host plant must be explicit.

technologies.summary: CO₂ is copolymerised with epoxides to make polycarbonates or polyether-carbonate polyols that partly replace fossil feedstock in polyurethanes.
technologies.carbon_fate: Bound in the polymer for the product's service life; end-of-life incineration releases it, landfill or recycling retains it longer. Not permanent storage.
chemical_reactions: n C₃H₆O + n CO₂ → [–CH(CH₃)CH₂O–C(O)O–]ₙ (propylene oxide copolymerisation)
catalysts: Double metal cyanide (DMC) catalysts; zinc and cobalt complexes
technologies.process_conditions: Moderate temperature and CO₂ pressure in liquid phase; catalyst choice controls CO₂ incorporation and cyclic carbonate by-product.

technical_performance.assumptions: Upper bound; commercial polyols incorporate substantially less CO₂ by mass

technologies.demonstrated_scale: CO₂-containing polyols have been produced industrially; volumes per site must be checked against producer disclosures.
known_limitations: Limited CO₂ mass fraction per tonne of product
Epoxide supply and its own emissions
Small total CO₂ volumes relative to emissions
technologies.economics: Value comes mainly from displacing more expensive epoxide feedstock, not from CO₂ consumption volume.
technologies.lifecycle_evidence: Benefits stem mostly from avoided fossil feedstock. Compare full cradle-to-gate polyol results, then account for end-of-life fate.

technologies.summary: Semiconductor photocatalysts use sunlight to drive CO₂ reduction with water directly, without a separate electrolyser.
technologies.carbon_fate: Most target products (CO, methane, methanol) are fuels or fuel precursors, so carbon is typically re-released at use.
catalysts: Semiconductors such as TiO₂ with co-catalysts; molecular and hybrid systems
technologies.process_conditions: Near-ambient temperature under illumination. Report light source, spectrum, irradiance, quantum yield, product rates and control experiments together.

technical_performance.assumptions: Electrons transferred per methane formed; sets the charge-carrier demand, not the efficiency

technologies.demonstrated_scale: Predominantly laboratory research; solar-to-fuel efficiencies reported so far are generally low.
known_limitations: Product separation from mixed, dilute streams
technologies.economics: No credible plant economics yet; reactor area per unit output is the key cost driver.
technologies.lifecycle_evidence: Lifecycle data is limited to early-stage estimates; materials and large reactor area dominate.

technologies.summary: CO₂ reacts with calcium- or magnesium-rich materials such as slags or concrete to form stable carbonates.
technologies.carbon_fate: Carbonate minerals are stable over geological timescales if not recalcined or acid-leached; durability is the strongest of any CCU route.
catalysts: No universal catalyst; mineral reactivity and conditioning control the process
technologies.process_conditions: Pressure, moisture and particle size depend on feedstock and product route.

technical_performance.assumptions: Complete carbonation of reactive CaO; real materials contain less reactive phase

technologies.demonstrated_scale: Route-specific; curing, aggregate production and waste treatment cannot share one readiness rating.
technologies.economics: Consider feedstock treatment, CO₂ delivery, product value and local transport rather than carbon uptake alone.
technologies.lifecycle_evidence: Carbonate retention may be durable, but net removal additionally requires atmospheric carbon and a complete lifecycle balance. Calcining virgin limestone can offset carbonation uptake.
